newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ analysts cautious over pulp price firming.
newsitem.headline: NZ analysts cautious over pulp price firming.

text.p: New Zealand forestry analysts expressed caution on Monday over recent rises in pulp and paper price signalled by several key U.S. industry players.

Last week the majors, including International Paper and Weyerhaeuser Co, confirmed widespread market talk that they were raising prices on some pulp grades by as much as $40 (U.S.) per tonne, mainly with effect from July 1.
Other firms planned to up paper and linerboard prices.
But Steve Cozens, forestry analyst at First NZ Capital, said he didn't expect the planned July price increases, effectively the second round of hikes within a month, to come through.
North American and Scandinavian (NorScan) pulp inventories fell by 103,000 tonnes in May, to 1.6 million tonnes, in a move usually interpreted as showing a better demand/supply balance.
Cozens argued this fall was less than expected and that it appeared to be more driven by a downturn in supply than an increase in demand.
Given that producers have already seen one price increase go through and were steeling for a second, he expected some would cancel scheduled downtime at their mills.
"In which case there is going to be a significant increase in production over the next little while," Cozens said.

"It just comes down to how much capacity you've got. If you've got excess capacity overhanging the market then fundamentally you've got excess supply. It's going to take some time before market demand catches up with that," he added.

Analysts agreed that it was clear that the pulp price has now bottomed out and this in itself justified the recent pick-up in the price of New Zealand forestry stocks led by Fletcher Paper and Carter Holt Harvey.
However, Cozens said he did not expect any significant upturn in pulp prices this year due to a fundamental supply/ demand imbalance that could only be changed by plant closures.
"But it's an industry that we don't see many closures (in) because not only are there high barriers to entry, there are high barriers to exit the industry," he said.

Analysts estimated that North American pulp mills are operating at just 75-80 percent capacity. They noted that domestic mills have also taken downtime, suggesting there is backed-up capacity here too.
But another analyst, John Cairns at Cavill White Securities, was more optimistic, saying he expected NorScan inventory levels to reach equilibrium at 1.5 million tonnes and he saw a fair outlook.
"It's just a clearing process taking place, so I think its pretty positive," he said.
"It's not just wishful thinking -- there are some really solid fundamentals behind these recent signalled price movements," he said.
"As the inventories are worked down, and now that they are getting back to equilibrium, that downtime can be withdrawn," he said.
Analysts estimate that for most operators, a break-even point is around in the upper US$400s to early $500s per tonne for pulp.

Current market levels vary around the world, and are seldom clearly defined for very long, but prices for softwood pulp are seen ranging through the upper $500s towards $600, with the U.S. producers targeting a move through to $630 next month.
